source: Curated from operator disclosures, trade press, and EIA country analysis briefs
methodology: Each refinery is assigned a Hormuz crude dependency score in [0, 1] based on (a) geographic bypass accessibility (Petroline / ADCOP), (b) historical feedstock slate disclosures, (c) whether the refinery's country commercially exits crude via Hormuz. Oman's Mina al Fahal and Sohar are explicitly scored LOW because they sit on the Gulf of Oman east of the strait and act as Hormuz hedges rather than dependents. Indian and Pakistani refineries are scored 0 because this layer is scoped to the Middle East regional physical map — their global-market exposure is real but modeled elsewhere. Scores are expert estimates, not measurements; refine them when operator assays land.

entries.note: ADNOC flagship at Ruwais. Fed by ADCOP (Habshan-Fujairah) which bypasses Hormuz entirely, so most feedstock survives a closure. Score held above 0.2 because a full Hormuz shut still tightens total volume availability given Upper Zakum offshore wells that currently route via Gulf outlets.
Coastal Khuzestan refinery on the Shatt al-Arab. Iran has no non-Hormuz export route and no bypass pipeline; Abadan is the archetypal Hormuz-locked asset.
Inland central Iran, fed by domestic pipeline from Ahvaz. Feedstock availability is indirect: an extended Hormuz closure collapses Iranian field production once storage fills.
Directly on the Hormuz chokepoint — as geographically exposed as any refinery in the region.
Inland, fed from Ahvaz via domestic trunk. Same logic as Arak — feedstock tightens once upstream storage fills.

Baghdad, fed by southern crude. A regional Hormuz closure locks Iraqi commerce system-wide.

Gulf of Oman, east of the Hormuz strait. Omani crude exits directly to the Arabian Sea without transiting Hormuz — this refinery is a Hormuz HEDGE, not a dependent. Score kept slightly above zero to account for intra-Gulf commercial spillover.

Sohar is on Oman's northern Gulf of Oman coast — east of Hormuz. Physical feedstock reaches it without transiting the strait. Scored 0.2 (not 0) because regional disruption tightens all Gulf balances.
Qatar's only refinery, on the Persian Gulf coast. Commercially Hormuz-locked; no bypass exists.

Saudi east-coast refinery at Jubail. Fed directly from Ghawar via domestic trunk — physically resilient — but exports exit through the Gulf, so commercial exposure is high. Petroline runs toward Yanbu, not inland, so no feedstock hedge.
Jeddah on the Red Sea. Fed via Petroline (East-West pipeline) which IS the Hormuz bypass. Minimal exposure.
Rabigh on the Red Sea. Petroline-fed. A full bypass saturation might tighten allocation vs. Yanbu but feedstock remains available.

Ras Tanura on the eastern Saudi coast. Crude is sourced locally from Ghawar, so physical feedstock is resilient, but the refinery's product exports and upstream storage fill through Hormuz. Score held high because the refinery's operational envelope collapses once exports are locked.
Inland central Saudi refinery serving the domestic market. Moderate exposure — feedstock is available but the broader Saudi logistics system balances through eastern export nodes.
Yanbu (SAMREF / Aramco). The literal terminal of Petroline — a 100% bypass-accessible refinery. Minimal Hormuz exposure.
YASREF (Aramco + Sinopec). Same physical Petroline terminus as SAMREF — fully bypass-accessible.
